walkthrough:
Sort RNA Bases Into Purines and Pyrimidines**
RNA contains four bases: A, G, C and U. Adenine and guanine have a larger double-ring structure and are called purines, while cytosine and uracil have a smaller single-ring structure and are called pyrimidines.

Read The Bases Shown**
Fig. 6.1 shows G, A, U and C on mRNA and U, A, G and C on tRNA. The purines among these are adenine and guanine.

hints: Focus on the loop labelled J at the bottom of the tRNA and think about what its three bases do - they match up with a triplet on the mRNA inside the ribosome.
walkthrough:
Link Structure To Matching Function**
Each tRNA has a triplet of exposed bases at one end that pairs with a complementary triplet on mRNA. The mRNA triplet is called a codon, and the matching triplet on tRNA that recognises it is called the anticodon.

hints: Find the next mRNA codon to the right of the ribosome that the incoming val-tRNA will sit over, then apply complementary pairing A-U and G-C to work out the tRNA triplet.
walkthrough:
Find The Next Codon**
The ribosome is moving to the right, so the incoming tRNA carrying val will pair with the next exposed codon GUC on the mRNA.

Apply Complementary Pairing**
In RNA, G pairs with C and U pairs with A. So GUC on mRNA pairs with CAG on the tRNA. That triplet at J is CAG.

hints: Recall the same type of weak bond that holds the two strands of DNA together between bases - the same bond temporarily holds codon to anticodon.
walkthrough:
Recall How Bases Hold Together**
Complementary bases do not form strong covalent bonds. They attract each other through weak hydrogen bonds, which can form and break easily as the ribosome moves.

Apply To Codon-Anticodon**
The three bases at J form hydrogen bonds with the complementary bases of the mRNA codon, holding the tRNA briefly in place for the amino acid to be added.
Final answer: by hydrogen bonds / hydrogen bonding between complementary bases
